title: The Illusion of Love
theme: God's love is everlasting, but our ability to express that love is shaped by our human experiences, limitations, and the passage of time.
opening: We spend our lives learning what love means. It changes as we grow older, as relationships deepen, and as we experience loss and disappointment. But what happens when we know the extraordinary love of God and realize we cannot always express that same love to others?
prayer: Heavenly Father,  Thank You for loving us with a love that never fades, never abandons us, and never depends upon our ability to understand it fully.  You know the disappointments, losses, and experiences that have shaped our hearts. You know how deeply we can love and how difficult it can sometimes be to express that love.  Lord Jesus, help me never to lose sight of the love You have made known to me. When my heart becomes guarded or weary, remind me that Your love remains within reach.  Teach me to recognize Your presence in others, as Paul asked Philemon to recognize a brother in Onesimus. Let the love I receive from You become a blessing in the lives of those around me.  And when I long for the fullness of Your Kingdom, remind me that You are already among us, guiding us toward the day when we will know Your love face to face.  May Your love continue to grow within me, even when I struggle to express it.  Amen.
body:
“We love because he first loved us.” — 1 John 4:19

Over the past couple of days, I have been thinking a great deal about love. Not simply the love we feel for our families or the people closest to us, but what love really is and how our understanding of it changes throughout our lives.

I have come to realize that loving others has become harder for me. Perhaps it is the losses and disappointments I have experienced, or perhaps it is simply the accumulation of years. I have wondered whether some of what we call love is an illusion, because it takes so many different forms and can change so dramatically over a lifetime.

The way we love as children is different from the way we love as young adults. As we grow older, love becomes intertwined with responsibilities, sacrifices, disappointments, and the necessity of letting go.

I think of my dogs and the immense love I feel for them. I care for their needs, protect them, and want them to know they have nothing to fear, that I will always care for them. I think of my children, whom I love just as deeply, but whom I have had to learn to release into their own lives. And I think of my husband, where love encompasses so many different aspects of a life shared together.

Then I think of my mother and sister, whom I will see this Thanksgiving. My mother has dementia now, and I know our time together will be different. Yet my love for her, and for my sister, encompasses decades of memories and experiences. It is almost impossible to put into words. That love transcends the changes that life has brought.

And above all of these is my love for God, for Jesus, and for the heavenly family and saints whose lives reveal such extraordinary devotion to Him.

What I have come to understand is that when we truly allow the love of God to be known to us, that love emanates from us. It becomes part of who we are and how we live. I know this love, yet I cannot always express it as fully as I know it within my soul.

Today's first reading from Philemon speaks to this.

Paul writes to Philemon about Onesimus, a man who had been enslaved to him. Paul asks Philemon to welcome Onesimus back, no longer merely as a slave, but as a beloved brother in Christ.

Then Paul says something that caught my attention: “May I profit from you in the Lord. Refresh my heart in Christ.”

Paul is asking Philemon to allow the love he has received from Christ to become visible in the way he receives Onesimus. Their earthly relationship may have been defined by master and slave, but Christ has introduced something greater. They are brothers in the Lord.

I find that beautiful because Paul is not simply speaking about the feeling of love. He is asking Philemon to live it.

And then, in today's Gospel, the Pharisees ask Jesus when the Kingdom of God will come.

How extraordinary that question seems to me. They are standing before Jesus, speaking with Him, listening to His words, and yet asking when God's Kingdom will arrive.

Jesus tells them, “For behold, the Kingdom of God is among you.”

They were looking for something that was already present in their midst.

Jesus then tells His disciples that a time will come when they will long to see one of the days of the Son of Man. He warns them not to run after those who claim He has appeared somewhere, explaining that His future revelation will be unmistakable, like lightning illuminating the sky.

I think about the disciples after His Ascension, longing to see Him again. And I think about us today, longing for the day when we will finally see Him face to face.

We know something of God's love now, but we have yet to experience its fullness.

Perhaps that is what I have been trying to understand about love. On earth, we experience it through so many different relationships, feelings, and expressions. Some endure, some change, and some leave us wounded. Yet the love of God is not temporary or superficial. It does not abandon us. It is more real and everlasting than we can fully comprehend in our earthly understanding.

I believe that in God's Kingdom we will finally experience and give love without the limitations that accompany our human lives. There will be no fear of losing it, no misunderstandings, and no uncertainty about whether it is real.

But Jesus reminds us that His Kingdom is already among us. We do not have to wait until heaven to begin experiencing His love or allowing it to reach others.

And perhaps this is what Paul is asking of Philemon, and what God continues to ask of us.

To receive His love and allow it to become visible in our lives, even when doing so is difficult.

I cannot always explain why loving others has become harder for me. I only know that the love I have experienced from God is greater than anything I can fully express.

And I am grateful that He continues to love me as I learn, imperfectly, to give that love to others.
